Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

Vignette:
Le Thi Anh had always taken pride in her work as a welder. She was meticulous, with a steady hand and an eye for detail that earned her respect from her colleagues at the shipyard. But on one fateful day six months ago, her attention lapsed for just a moment - and she accidentally triggered a spark that set off a chain reaction of events, resulting in a serious injury to her coworker. The memory of that day still haunted Anh, not just because of what happened, but also due to the fragmented nature of her recollection. She could vividly recall the acrid smell of burnt metal and the bitter taste of ozone on her tongue - sensations that would suddenly flood back whenever she encountered certain stimuli, like the hum of a welding torch or the smell of hot steel. But there were gaps in her memory too, holes that left her with more questions than answers about what exactly had gone wrong. As time passed, Anh found herself becoming increasingly withdrawn and isolated. She started avoiding social gatherings and stopped attending meetings at work, fearing she would run into the injured coworker or be asked to talk about the accident. Her mind became preoccupied with self-blame, replaying over and over in her head all the things she could have done differently that day. If only she had double-checked the welding equipment; if only she had been more alert... Her guilt-ridden ruminations made it hard for Anh to sleep at night. She would lie awake, reliving the events leading up to the accident and replaying conversations with her coworker in her head. Her concentration suffered as a result, making everyday tasks feel like insurmountable challenges. Even simple things like grocery shopping or taking public transportation became daunting experiences, as she found herself constantly on edge, anticipating potential dangers. When something did remind Anh of the accident - like the screech of tires or the smell of smoke - her body would react with a surge of adrenaline, leaving her heart racing and her palms sweating. These physical reactions were intense and overwhelming, making it hard for her to shake off the feeling that she was walking on eggshells all the time. Anh's avoidance behaviors had started to take a toll on her relationships at work too. Her colleagues noticed her withdrawal and tried to reach out, but Anh couldn't bring herself to talk about what happened or how she was really feeling. She became increasingly isolated in her small apartment, barely leaving except for essential errands or shifts at the shipyard. What finally brought Anh to seek help was a run-in with her supervisor, who had noticed her declining performance and confronted her about it. For the first time since the accident, Anh felt like she couldn't just "get by" anymore - that her life was spiraling out of control in ways she couldn't manage on her own. As she sat in her therapist's office, she voiced a deep-seated fear: that she would never be able to shake off the weight of guilt and shame that had come to define her since that fateful day.
